--- engine: knitr filters: - webr webr: show-startup-message: true cell-options: autorun: true --- # Negotiation and Conflict Management ## Learning Objectives By the end of this chapter you will be able to: 1. **Identify** what a project manager negotiates and with whom. 2. **Prepare** for a negotiation: interests vs. positions, BATNA, reservation point, ZOPA. 3. **Apply** the principled-negotiation mindset (separate people from problem; focus on interests; win-win or no win). 4. **Determine** whether a zone of possible agreement exists and how wide it is. 5. **Classify** project conflict (goal-oriented, administrative, interpersonal) and its organizational vs. interpersonal causes. 6. **Select** a conflict-resolution method (confronting, compromising, withdrawal, smoothing, forcing) for a situation. 7. **Score** a multi-criteria supplier choice.
Before we begin: recall a negotiation you "won" but regretted Did you win the point and lose the relationship? Most project negotiations are with people you will work with again next week. That constraint changes everything.
## Introduction: the project manager negotiates every day As a project manager your day is full of negotiation, inside and outside the organization. You negotiate for or with: - **Resources** --- material, time, equipment, money - **Contractors** --- costs, delivery schedules, quality of material, hours of work - **Department managers** --- manpower, schedules On the RC-vehicle project the sharp negotiations are obvious: the **motor and control-system supply contract** (trusted MCS, now moving production to Mexico, vs. unproven Paragon four hours away with staff negotiating a first labour contract), and the recurring fight with **functional managers** over which engineers you get and for how long. ::: {.callout-note} **Industry snapshot.** An automotive buyer negotiating a multi-year harness contract is really negotiating the *whole package* --- price, tooling ownership, capacity guarantees, engineering support, payment terms. A defense subcontract negotiation is bounded by regulation (allowable cost, audit rights). In a food company, the PM negotiating a sanitation window with operations is negotiating *downtime*, which is money. :::
## The negotiation mindset - **Separate the people from the problem.** Everyone has ego, fears, insecurities --- do not tap into the other side's, or you lose control of both sides. - **Stick to business.** Keep personalities out of it; a charm offensive fools no one. - **Put yourself in their shoes.** Nobody likes a direct attack; it is counter-productive. - **Win-win or no win.** Talk money **last** if possible; a negotiation is about the whole package, not just the number. ## Getting ready There are three stages --- **before, during, after** --- and **before should be the biggest.** **Gather information about the other side:** their vital interests, goals, costs, strategies, positions, needs; their product strengths; concession patterns; past negotiating style; their **bottom line**; corporate deadlines and time constraints; their **budget**; geographic limits. Also know your own position, the players, and **who holds the power** --- including people behind the scenes. **Develop strategy:** aim high (with more than one win-win scenario in mind); be realistic; rank your objectives by priority; know your **bottom line**; decide whether deadlock or termination are tolerable outcomes; separate the **necessary** items from the **expendable**; have a few **red herrings** ready; plan how to help the other side sell the deal internally; find where your interests and theirs intersect. **Write the plan and an agenda:** your interests and theirs; your desired outcomes and your estimate of theirs; your authority limits and theirs; any fact sheet either side needs. The agenda names the meeting's goal, is published in advance, and lists invitees and location. ### The three questions --- and who controls the room Every negotiator should ask: **How much power do I have? What time pressure is there? Do I trust the other side?** And: *who controls a conversation?* **Generally the person asking the questions**, because they set the direction. Aim to ask most of the questions --- politely --- and recognise when it is being done to you. ## BATNA, reservation point, and ZOPA - **BATNA** --- your Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement. What you will do if this deal falls through. A strong BATNA is your real source of power. - **Reservation point** --- the worst deal you would still accept (a buyer's *maximum* price, a seller's *minimum* price), set by your BATNA. - **ZOPA** --- the Zone Of Possible Agreement: the overlap between the two reservation points. If there is no overlap, **no deal is possible** at those terms. ### Worked Example 1: is there a ZOPA? You are buying the motor/controller package. Your BATNA (Paragon's quote plus the cost of the risk it carries) puts your **reservation price at \$168 000** --- you would not pay MCS more than that. MCS's floor, given their costs and other customers, is **\$150 000**. Live cell --- move either side's reservation price and see whether a deal still exists. ```{webr-r} #| label: zopa-example-10 buyer_reservation <- 168000 # most you will pay seller_reservation <- 150000 # least they will accept if (seller_reservation <= buyer_reservation) { zopa_low <- seller_reservation zopa_high <- buyer_reservation cat(sprintf("ZOPA exists: $%s to $%s (width $%s)\n", format(zopa_low, big.mark = " "), format(zopa_high, big.mark = " "), format(zopa_high - zopa_low, big.mark = " "))) cat("Any agreed price in that band beats both sides' alternatives.\n") } else { cat("No ZOPA -- the seller's floor is above the buyer's ceiling. Change the package or walk.\n") } ``` ### Try it yourself: reservation points from a BATNA ```{webr-r} #| label: zopa-calc-10 # Buyer's side: BATNA is Paragon at $150k, but carrying $25k of extra risk cost. paragon_price <- 150000 paragon_risk <- 25000 buyer_reservation <- paragon_price + paragon_risk # indifference point vs MCS # Seller's side (MCS): cost to make + minimum acceptable margin. mcs_cost <- 132000 mcs_margin <- 15000 seller_reservation <- mcs_cost + mcs_margin cat(sprintf("Buyer reservation (max) : $%s\n", format(buyer_reservation, big.mark = " "))) cat(sprintf("Seller reservation (min) : $%s\n", format(seller_reservation, big.mark = " "))) if (seller_reservation <= buyer_reservation) { cat(sprintf("ZOPA width: $%s -- a deal is possible.\n", format(buyer_reservation - seller_reservation, big.mark = " "))) cat(sprintf("A midpoint settlement would be about $%s.\n", format(round((buyer_reservation + seller_reservation) / 2), big.mark = " "))) } else { cat("No ZOPA. Improve your BATNA, expand the package, or walk away.\n") } ```
Why does improving your BATNA move the whole negotiation? Your reservation point is set by your BATNA. If you pre-qualify a credible second supplier (a better BATNA), your reservation price drops --- you can credibly walk at a lower number --- which shifts the ZOPA and the likely settlement in your favour, *without* saying a word at the table. The best negotiating move often happens before the meeting, in the form of a real alternative.
## Language and tells A few sample moves: *"My colleagues and I cannot settle for that"* (establish power early); *"What are you looking for in these negotiations?"* (make them open first); *"Do you have the authority to commit to that?"* (probe their authority); *"Let's set that aside and come back to it"* (avoid a hard no). And listen past the words. *"To be brutally honest..."* and *"To tell you the truth..."* often precede a lie. *"Off the record..."* --- nothing is off the record; the negotiation is always on. Watch **congruence**: when words and body language disagree, believe the body language. ## Conflict management Conflict *"begins when you perceive that someone has frustrated, or is about to frustrate, a major concern of yours."* It is **perceptual** (it doesn't matter whether a wrong was actually done, only that it is perceived) and **dynamic** (the original cause may no longer matter, yet the conflict persists). Three types on projects: - **Goal-oriented** --- disagreement over end results, scope outcomes, specs, priorities. Fuelled by vague goals that let people fill in their own interpretation (and hidden agendas). - **Administrative** --- who has authority or control over functions, tasks, and decisions. The **matrix** structure breeds this --- everyone has two bosses. - **Interpersonal** --- personality differences: work ethic, behavioural style, ego, personalities that don't mesh. ### Three views of conflict | School | View | Response | |---|---|---| | **Traditional** | All conflict is bad | Suppress and eliminate it, fast | | **Behavioral** | Conflict is natural and inevitable | Accept it and manage it well | | **Interactionist** | A *controlled* amount of conflict is *beneficial* | Encourage some --- it prevents stagnation and drives innovation; too little = inertia, too much = chaos | ### Sources, ranked by intensity ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Sources of project conflict ranked by typical intensity (from PMBOK data). Schedules, priorities, and resources dominate; personality is last -- it is usually the first thing blamed and rarely the real cause.](10-Negotiation-and-Conflict-Management_files/figure-html/fig-conflict-sources-10-1.png){#fig-conflict-sources-10 fig-align='center' width=912} ::: ::: **Organizational causes:** reward systems (functional managers hoard their best people), scarce resources, uncertainty (weak matrix --- unclear who is in charge), different mindsets among departments. **Interpersonal causes:** misconceptions about others' behaviour, faulty communication (often *style*, not content), personal grudges. > *"It only becomes personal when the root cause of the conflict is not > resolved. Personality is very frequently the first diagnosis"* --- and usually > the wrong one. ### Conflict-resolution methods (PMBOK) | Method | What it is | Best when | |---|---|---| | **Confronting** (problem-solving) | Solve the real, underlying problem | There is time and goodwill; the durable fix | | **Compromising** | Each side gives something; partial satisfaction for both | Positions are far apart and a deadline looms | | **Withdrawal / avoidance** | Retreat or postpone | The issue is trivial, or emotions need to cool | | **Smoothing** | Emphasize agreement, play down differences | Preserving the relationship matters more right now | | **Forcing** | Push one view at the other's expense | A true emergency, or a matter of safety/ethics | ### Try it yourself: score the supplier choice Multi-criteria scoring turns "MCS feels safer" into a defensible number. ```{webr-r} #| label: supplier-scoring-10 criteria <- c("Quality record", "Delivery reliability", "Price", "Technical capability", "Supply-chain risk") weight <- c(0.30, 0.25, 0.15, 0.15, 0.15) # must sum to 1 # Score each supplier 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent) on each criterion. mcs <- c(5, 4, 3, 3, 2) # trusted, but production moving to Mexico paragon <- c(3, 3, 4, 5, 3) # unproven, new tech, plant 4 h away, labour talks mcs_total <- sum(weight * mcs) paragon_total <- sum(weight * paragon) tab <- data.frame(Criterion = criteria, Weight = weight, MCS = mcs, Paragon = paragon) print(tab, row.names = FALSE) cat(sprintf("\nWeighted score MCS: %.2f Paragon: %.2f\n", mcs_total, paragon_total)) cat(sprintf("Recommended: %s\n", ifelse(mcs_total >= paragon_total, "MCS", "Paragon"))) cat("Change the weights to your project's priorities and watch the answer move.\n") ``` ## Key Takeaways - PMs negotiate constantly --- for resources, with contractors, with functional managers. **Before** is the biggest stage; prepare more than you think you need. - **Separate people from the problem**, focus on **interests** not positions, aim for **win-win or no win**, and talk money last. - **BATNA** sets your **reservation point**; the overlap of both reservation points is the **ZOPA**. No ZOPA, no deal --- improve your BATNA or change the package. - The person **asking the questions** usually controls the conversation. - Project conflict is **perceptual and dynamic**. Types: **goal-oriented, administrative, interpersonal**. The **interactionist** view holds that a controlled amount of conflict is healthy. - Teams fight most about **schedules, priorities, and resources** --- **personality** is last and is usually a misdiagnosis of an unresolved root cause. - Match the resolution method --- **confronting, compromising, withdrawal, smoothing, forcing** --- to the situation; confronting is the durable fix. ## Practice Problems
Problem 1: Name the cause of conflict Which cause does each statement point to? 1. "I can't talk to her after what her son said to my son." → **Personal grudge** (interpersonal). 2. "Sales management here are lazy --- they always leave by 4:00." → **Different mindsets among departments** (organizational). 3. "She barely looked at my report; she's already decided to ignore it." → **Misconceptions about others' behaviour** (interpersonal). 4. "Our computers are slow because their division always gets the best ones." → **Scarce resources** (organizational). 5. "The worse your project does at year-end, the better mine looks." → **Reward systems** (organizational). 6. "Why should I do that for the PM if my functional manager didn't tell me?" → **Uncertainty / two bosses** (organizational, matrix).
Problem 2: ZOPA and a walk-away You will pay at most \$95 000 for a tooling package (your BATNA: build it in-house for \$98 000). The vendor's floor is \$102 000. (a) Is there a ZOPA? (b) What are your options? **Solution.** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} buyer_max <- 95000 seller_min <- 102000 cat(ifelse(seller_min <= buyer_max, "ZOPA exists", "No ZOPA"), "\n") cat(sprintf("Gap to close: $%s\n", format(seller_min - buyer_max, big.mark = " "))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` No ZOPA Gap to close: $7 000 ``` ::: ::: (a) No --- the vendor's floor is \$7 000 above your ceiling. (b) Exercise your BATNA (build in-house at \$98 000), expand the package so the vendor's per-unit economics improve, split tooling ownership, or find a third vendor.
Problem 3 (discussion): the functional manager skips your stand-up The maintenance supervisor on your project has missed the first two morning meetings. How could this signal *each* of: reward systems, scarce resources, uncertainty, different mindsets, misconceptions, faulty communication, personal grudge? **Discussion points.** *Reward systems*: their boss doesn't value project work, so they deprioritize it. *Scarce resources*: they are triple-booked and the meeting lost. *Uncertainty*: they are not sure the meeting applies to them. *Different mindsets*: maintenance culture sees planning meetings as talk, not work. *Misconceptions*: they think you have already sidelined their input. *Faulty communication*: the invite never reached them, or the time was ambiguous. *Grudge*: a past project soured them on you. The point: **do not jump to the grudge** --- confront it by asking, and you will usually find one of the structural causes.
